title: Shipping emissions caused almost $1trn in global economic damages, analysis finds
summary: Shipping's dirty footprint is undeniable: new analysis reveals the sector's 19,029 million tonnes of CO2 emissions from 1990-2020 inflicted nearly $1 trillion in global economic damages. These costs disproportionately impact lower-income nations, a stark reminder of the industry's continued reliance on high-carbon fuels and its externalized environmental burden. The IMO's slow-moving "Net Zero Framework," still unadopted in 2025, offers little credible action against this documented climate liability, highlighting a severe lack of urgency.
content:
This is according to an analysis by Zero Carbon Analytics (ZCA), which calculated the economic damages by combining historical international shipping emissions data from the IMO with a climate damage calculator developed by Stanford researchers.

The analysis used cumulative shipping emissions of 19,029 million tonnes of CO2 between 1990 and 2020, applying a model that links CO2 emissions to rising global temperatures and temperature increases to changes in GDP growth.

Using a 2% discount rate, the model estimated total global economic damages of $962.7bn. To allocate these damages between countries, ZCA used country-level estimates from the model’s damage map, calculated each country’s share of global climate damages and applied those proportions to the shipping-related total.

As per the analysis, the US experienced the largest estimated economic impact, at $280.7bn, followed by China at $113.5bn and Japan at $66.8bn. However, when measured against national economic output, the effects were greater in several lower-income countries and Middle Eastern economies.

The analysis estimates that shipping-related climate damages reduced the UAE’s 2020 gross domestic product by 0.35%, Saudi Arabia’s by 0.34%, Mali’s by 0.32% and Burkina Faso’s by 0.30%.

Shipping decarbonisation framework

International shipping accounts for around 2% of global carbon dioxide emissions. In 2018, carbon dioxide represented a little more than 98% of total emissions from shipping, including international, domestic and fishing activities.

The International Maritime Organisation (IMO) adopted emissions reduction targets in 2023, committing the sector to cut annual greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by at least 20% by 2030 and at least 70% by 2040, compared with 2008 levels. The targets also aim for net-zero emissions by or around 2050.

The proposed Net Zero Framework was approved in April 2025 but has not been formally adopted. It would establish the first global, legally binding, industry-wide mechanism combining emissions limits with GHG pricing.

Disagreements over implementation costs and political tensions have delayed its adoption.

The financial debate has focused on the cost of introducing the framework.

An IMO assessment estimates that a policy mechanism similar to the proposed framework would cost $13.78trn between 2023 and 2050, compared with $9.62trn under a business-as-usual scenario.

The difference is $4.16trn, although the assessment includes investment in ships and other expenditure that may be reinvested in the industry.

ZCA argues that the cost of inaction must also be considered. Its analysis estimates that implementing the framework and achieving net-zero by 2050 could avoid approximately 14.2 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions between 2026 and 2050, compared with business as usual.

The reduction could prevent an estimated 1.5 million excess deaths from climate-related temperature impacts by 2100. It could also reduce exposure to unprecedented heat for around eight million people by 2070.

The analysis further estimates that the avoided warming could help prevent the loss of approximately 260 million additional coral colonies on the Great Barrier Reef under conditions similar to the mass bleaching event in 2016.

ZCA warns that the economic consequences of continued shipping emissions are likely to increase as climate impacts worsen, while highlighting the unequal distribution of those damages, with countries that have contributed relatively little to global emissions facing a disproportionate share of the economic burden.

The findings come ahead of a series of meetings at the IMO, where member states will discuss the proposed Net Zero Framework, which would introduce emissions limits and GHG pricing across the international shipping industry.

The meetings are scheduled to take place between 23 November and 4 December.
